abstract.p: The instant invention teaches pathogenic SHIV which cause AIDS in monkeys, the construction of virus for use in vaccines against pathogenic SHIV and HIV-1, and methods for prophylactic and therapeutic vaccination to prevent or inhibit HIV-1 infection and/or disease. The instant invention teaches the construction of modified live virus for use in vaccines against HIV-1, and methods for prophylactic and therapeutic vaccination to prevent or inhibit HIV-1 infection and/or disease. The instant invention teaches the use of viral DNA vaccines for the treatment and prevention of HIV infection and/or disease.

description.p: Live Virus Vaccines to Protect Primates from HIV-1 Infection and Disease
Related Applications

This application is a Continuation-in-part of U.S. Provisional Patent Application Serial number 60/102,143, filed September 28, 199808/850,492; and U.S. Patent Application Serial No. 09/071,066 filed April 30, 1998, which is a continuation in part of 08/958,410 filed October 29, 1997, which is a continuation in part of 08/850,492 filed May 2, 1997, which is a continuation in part of 08/442,010 filed May 16, 1995, now U.S. Patent No. 5,849,994, all hereby incorporated by reference in its entirety.
Statement of Government Rights
This work was supported in part by NIH grant numbers AI38492 and RR06753, the Government of the United States of America may have rights in this invention.
Field of the Invention

This invention relates to the field of prophylactic and therapeutic vaccines for generating protection from HIV-1 induced disease and infection, and compositions and methods for such vaccination, and compositions and methods for the therapeutic treatment of HIV- 1 infected individuals.
Background of the Invention

It is recognized that effective vaccines which will inhibit or prevent HIV-1 infection or induced disease in humans will be useful for the treatment of certain high-risk populations, and as a general prophylactic vaccination for the general population that may risk HIV-1 infection or HIV-1 induced disease. A vaccine that will confer long-term protection against the transmission of HIV-1 would be most useful. Unfortunately, numerous problems stand in the way of developing effective vaccines for the prevention of HIV-1 infection and disease. Certain problems are most likely the result of the unique nature of the HIV-1 virus and its functional properties, and as yet no effective vaccine has been developed (for review see:
Berzofsky et al., Developing Synthetic Peptide Vaccines for HIV-1, Vaccines 95, pps. 135- 142, 1995; Cease and Berzofsky, Toward a Vaccine for AIDS: The Emergence of Immunobiology-Based Vaccine Design, Annual Review of Immunology 12:923-989, 1994; Berzofsky, Progress towards Artificial Vaccines for HIV, Vaccines 92, pps. 41-50, 1992).
There is a Need for an Effective Vaccine

The theoretical basis for the development of an effective HIV-1 vaccine is the fact that in nearly all viral infections, certain segments of an infected population recover and become immune to future viral infection by the same pathogen. Examples of typical viral pathogens include measles, poliomyelitis, chicken pox, hepatitis B, small pox, etc. Thus, it is assumed that protective immunity against HIV-1 virus can be conferred on primate populations via a properly designed vaccine. The high mortality rate of HIV-1 infection, and the apparently extremely rare incidence of recovery and protective immunity against HIV-1 infection has cast doubt on the ability of primates to generate natural immunity to HIV- 1 infection when the pathogenic HIV-1 is the un-modified wild-type viral pathogen. Thus, significant resistance remains as to the possibility of creating an effective HIV-1 vaccine via human- modification of pathogenic virus.

A hallmark measure of resistance to future viral infection, is the generation of "neutralizing antibodies" to the virus pathogen, and cellular immunity against infected cells. In typical viral infections, the generation of neutralizing antibodies and cellular immunity by the infected individual's immune system heralds recovery from infection. However, in HIV-1 infection, neutralizing antibodies and cellular immunity appear very early during the infection, and have been associated with only a transient decrease in viral burden. In HIV-1 infection, in spite of the generation of neutralizing antibodies and cellular immunity, viral replication rebounds and AIDS (acquired immune deficiency syndrome) develops. Thus in HIV-1 infected people, neutralizing antibodies and cellular immunity are not accurate measures of protective immunity. However, induction and maintenance of these arms of the immune response by vaccine may prevent infection by the virus under natural conditions.
A further problem in developing an effective vaccine for HIV-1 that has concerned researchers is the antigenic diversity of the wild-type virus. It has been believed to be a strong possibility that vaccines generated via recombinant HIV-1 coat proteins will confer resistance only to specific phenotypes of virus, and not provide broad spectrum immunity.

Currently, vaccine development using recombinant HIV-1 gpl20 peptide, a viral coat protein of HIV-1, has passed phase-one clinical trials showing no toxicity. However, data indicated that neutralizing antibodies appeared only transiently. Thus, recombinant HIV-1 gpl20 peptide vaccines may only act in the short-term, with subsequent reversion to susceptibility of infection.
The Fear of Live Virus Vaccines

In general, it is accepted that live-virus vaccines induce better immunity against pathogenic viruses than isolated viral proteins (see for example Putkonen et al., Immuization with Live Attenuated SIVmac Can Protect Macaques against Mucosal Infection with SIVsm, Vaccines 96, pps. 20-210, 1996; Dimmock and Primrose Introduction to Modern Virology, 4th Ed., Blackwell Science, 1994). However, the use of live lentivirus vaccines, such as HIV-1 vaccine, is resisted because of great concern that the vaccine virus will persist indefinitely in the inoculated population because of the integration of viral DNA into the host DNA of the inoculated individuals (see for example ten Haaft et al., Evidence of Circulating Pathogenic SIV following Challenge of Macaques Vaccinated with Live Attenuated SIV, Vaccines 96, pps. 219-224, 1996). Thus, a safe, and effective vaccine against HIV-1 will encompass modifications to prevent the development of virulent pathogenic infection that could occur by either random mutation or other change to the initially non-pathogenic vaccine virus.
Model Systems for Testing Vaccines

Since testing of vaccine efficacy requires vaccine inoculation then challenge of the subject with infectious virus, it is ethically and practically difficult to attempt preliminary studies using human subjects. The use of model systems for preliminary design and testing of
candidate vaccines has been hampered by various species specific features of the viruses. Apart from humans, HIV-1 itself is currently known to replicate only in certain rare and endangered chimpanzees. The feasibility of obtaining sufficient numbers of such endangered animals for a full preliminary study of HIV-1 virus vaccines is quite low. It is much more preferable to prepare initial studies using validated analogous animal model systems.

One analogous model system for HIV-1 infection has been the SIVmac system (Simian Immunodeficiency Virus, macaque) and infection of macaque monkeys. Deletion of the regulatory gene nef rendered SIVmac a virulent. However, SIVnιac is only an analogous model system for human HIV-1 infection, and does not replicate all of the salient features of HIV-1 infection/disease of humans (see generally Hu et al., Transmembrane Protein and Core Antigens in Protection against SIV Infection, Vaccines 95, pps. 167-173, 1995; Lewis and Johnson, Developing animal models for AIDS research - progress and problems, TIBTECH 13:142-150, 1995; Desrosiers, The Simian Immunodeficiency Viruses, Annual Review of Immunology 8:557-578, 1990). Researchers have also developed chimeric SIV-HIV chimeric virus, placing the envelope proteins of HIV-1 on a background of SIVmac, which proved infectious to monkeys, but did not result in full-blown AIDS or an accurate model to mimic HIV-1 infection in monkeys (see generally Shibata and Adachi, SIV/HIV recombinants and their use in studying biological properties, AIDS Research and Human Retroviruses 8(3):403-409, 1992; Sakuragi et al., Infection of macaque monkeys with a chimeric human and simian immunodeficiency virus, J. General Virology 73:2983-2987, 1992).

The recent development, by the present inventor, of highly pathogenic strains of SHIV, SHIVKLM, and SHIVKU_2, provided a new model for the study of HIV infection and disease which corresponds to the human disease much more accurately than any other previous model. U.S. Patent 5,849,994 (incorporated by reference in its entirety) describes this development and validation of a monkey model for human HIV infection and AIDS. This development of a new truly pathogenic virus which induces full-blown AIDS in monkeys, and the identification of the genetic basis for certain aspects of pathogenicity,
allows for the full scale efficient preparation and evaluation of HIV-1 vaccines, supported by in vivo data. As described below, the present invention teaches specific methods and virus constructs which are effective in generating an immune response in a vaccinated host to virus. Thus the present invention teaches constructs and methods for the effective in vivo therapeutic and/or prophylactic vaccination of mammals to inhibit or prevent HIV infection and/or related disease.

Brief Summary of the Invention

The present invention teaches an avirulent HIV-1 virus, wherein the vpu gene of the HIV-1 virus has been rendered non-functional or deleted. In addition to the non-functional vpu gene, the HIV-1 virus may have a non-functional or deleted nef gene. The instant
invention also encompasses a HIV-1 /HIV-2 chimeric virus wherein the chimeric DNA comprises HIV-2 LTR, gag, pol, and nef 'genes and HIV-1 env, tat, rev, vpu genes, where said vpu gene is rendered non-functional or is deleted. In a further embodiment the nef gene is optionally rendered non-functional or deleted. The instant invention also encompasses an avirulent SIV/HIV-1 chimeric virus, having a SIV LTR, gag, pol, and nef genes and HIV-1 env, tat, rev, vpu genes, where said vpu gene is rendered non-functional or deleted. In a further embodiment the nef gene is optionally rendered non-functional or deleted.

The instant invention embodies vaccines which inhibit the infection of cells by HIV-1, comprising a virus wherein the DNA of said virus comprises DNA consisting of HIV-2 LTR, gag, pol, and nef genes and HIV-1 env, tat, rev, vpu genes, where said vpu gene is rendered non- functional. In one embodiment the vpu gene is rendered non-functional by deletion. In a further embodiment the nef gene is optionally rendered non-functional or deleted.

In a further embodiment, the instant invention teaches vaccines which inhibits the infection of cells by HIV-1, comprising a virus wherein the DNA of said virus comprises DNA consisting of HIV-2 LTR, gag, pol, and nef genes and HIV-1 env, tat, rev genes, and no HIV-1 vpu gene.

A further embodiment of the invention encompasses vaccines which inhibit the infection of cells by HIV- 1 , comprising a virus wherein the DNA of said virus comprises HIV-1 DNA wherein the vpu gene of HIV-1 has been rendered non-functional. In one form, the vpu gene is rendered non-functional by deletion.
Thus the instant invention teaches vaccines which inhibit the infection of cells by HIV-1, comprising a virus wherein the DNA of said virus comprises HIV-1 DNA, and no vpu gene of HIV-1.

Another embodiment of the invention encompasses a vaccine which inhibits infection of cells by such a SIV/HIV-1 chimeric virus such as SHINKU.„ which comprises said virus wherein the vpu gene is rendered non-functional or deleted, in a suitable carrier. In another embodiment of the invention, such a vaccine contains said virus wherein the nef gene is optionally rendered non-functonal or deleted.
In accordance to the teaching of the instant invention, the disclosure teaches methods for inoculating a subject to inhibit virus infection by chimeric SHIV/HIV-1 virus such as SHIVKU_,, comprising administering a vaccine containing a modified virus, the DNA of said virus comprising DNA consisting of SIV LTR, gag, pol, and nef genes and HIV-1 env, tat, rev, vpu genes, where said vpu gene is non-functional. In another embodiment of the invention, such a vaccine contains said virus wherein the nef gene is optionally rendered non- functonal or deleted.

Further, the instant invention teaches methods for inoculating a subject to inhibit virus infection by HIV-1 comprising administering a vaccine containing a modified virus, the DNA of said virus comprising DNA consisting of HIV-2 LTR, gag, pol, and nef genes and HIV-1 env, tat, rev, vpu genes, where said vpu gene is non-functional. In a preferred embodiment, the vpu gene is deleted. In another embodiment of the invention, such a vaccine contains said virus wherein the nef gene is optionally rendered non-functonal or deleted.

Also encompassed by the instant invention are methods for inoculating a subject to inhibit virus infection by HIV-1 comprising administering a vaccine containing a modified virus, the DNA of said virus comprising DNA consisting of HIV-1 DNA, where the HIV-1 vpu gene is non-functional. In a preferred embodiment the vpu gene is deleted. In another embodiment of the invention, such a vaccine contains said virus wherein the nef gene is optionally rendered non- functional or deleted. The present invention also embodies the administration of viral DNA of the present invention directly to the subject to be treated. Such administration being made with DNA suspended in saline or other suitable carrier or packaging.

In a broad aspect, the instant invention provides for a general method for the creation of effective vaccines for conveying immunity to HIV-1 virus, wherein the virus is manipulated to impede its ability to effectively replicate and/or accumulate in the infected/inoculated host. Wherein one embodiment of this method is the perturbation of the activity of the vpu gene or gene product in the virus, or during host-virus interaction. In a further embodiment of the invention, the instant invention embodies the treatment of
currently infected HIV-1 positive patients to prevent further HIV-1 infection and/or continuing HIV- 1 infection.
Thus the present invention teaches constructs and methods for the effective in vivo therapeutic and/or prophylactic vaccination of mammals to inhibit or prevent HIV infection and/or related disease.
Description of the Invention

Development of a truly pathogenic virus that generates full-blown AIDS in monkeys is described in U.S. Patent No. 5,849,994. This pathogenic virus, named SHIVKU_, (originally isolated as PPc and PNb) is the first virus bearing the envelope of HIV-1 which can cause AIDS in a non-human primate, as indicated by a) all animals lost CD4" T cells during the first three weeks after inoculation with the virus (an excellent marker for virus pathogenicity); b) the virus is predictably pathogenic, with 70% of inoculated animals developing AIDS within six months (and thus vaccine efficacy can be evaluated in a short time using this monkey model system); and c) the virus invades across mucosal surfaces and causes AIDS after deposition in the mouth or in the vagina (thus allowing for evaluation of testing for efficacy against sexual transmission). This is truly a pathogenic, virulent virus which infects cells and causes HIV-1 like infection and disease in a monkey. The DNA of the virus was constructed of SIV LTR, gag, pol, and nef genes and HIV-1 env, tat, rev, vpu genes. Development of pathogenic SHIVKU_, was accomplished by sequential passage of virus through bone marrow using an SHIV construct containing the tat, rev, vpu, and env genes derived from a laboratory strain of HIV-1 (see also Joag et al., Chimeric Simian/Human Immunodeficiency Virus That Causes Progressive Loss of CD4+ T Cells and AIDS in Pig-Tailed Macaques, J. Virology 70(5):3189-3197, 1996). The virulent variant of SHIV was obtained after four passages as described in Narayan in U.S. Patent No. 5,849,994, and is summarized in Figure 5. Briefly, SHIV passaged through Rhesus macaque bone marrow was then further passaged through pig-tailed macaque bone marrow, resulting in a pathogenic SHIV, isolated from animal PNb and now named SHIVKU.,. Virus passaged an
additional time through a Rhesus macaque resulted in a pathogenic SHIV, isolated from animal 14A, now named SHIVKU_2. Virus isolated from animal PPc, a pig-tailed macaque was not pathogenic.

Examination of the genes of the virulent variant yielded information as to the genetic basis of the acquired virulence and pathogenicity. It was found that three genes had undergone several mutations during the passages and acquisition of virulence. Manipulation of genes can be routinely perfoπned using standard molecular biology and virology techniques (see for example Short Protocols in Molecular Biology. 2nd Edition, A Compendium of Methods from Current Protocols in Molecular Biology. (Eds. Ausubel et al., John Wiley & Sons, New York, 1992); Sambrook et al., 1989, Molecular Cloning - A Laboratory Manual 2nd. Ed., CSH Laboratory Press, New York).

It has been found that the vpu gene, present in the original SHIV as a non-functional gene, became functional in the SHIVKL . The vpu gene is an accessory gene found only in HIV-1. (for review see Vaishnav and Wong-Staal, The Biochemistry of AIDS, Annual Review of Biochemistry 60:577-630, 1991). It has been found that the env gene of HIV-1 in the pathogenic SHIV contained ten consensus mutations, and the nef gene of SIV in the SHIV had five mutations.

The results indicate that the vaccine virus of the invention are somehow impeded in the ability to replicate or accumulate efficiently, and as such the immune system of the inoculated host is able to respond to this viral challenge as if to any other virus, by mounting an appropriate, effective and thus immunity-conferring response. Thus the treatment of currently infected HIV-1 positive patients with agents that will interfere with the HIV-1 vpu gene or gene product can be effective therapeutics for modulating the effects of HIV-1 infection and/or continuing HIV-1 infection. Such agents can be either chemical, antibody based, or some other form of bioactive molecule.

The vpu gene of HIV-1 and the nef gene of SIVmac are thought to encode for nonstructural regulatory proteins. Deletion of both these genes from the SHIVKU_, molecular construct resulted in a first vaccine virus called Δ2 SHIV (Δ2 SHIV -4). A second vaccine
was made using a virus which incorporated the env and nef genes taken from the SHIVKU_, virus, and deleted only the vpu gene, this virus construct being named Avpu SHIVKU_, (Avpu SHIV-PPc) It has been found that Avpu SHIVKU_, (Avpu SHIV-PPc) replicates more vigorously than Δ2 SHIV in macaque tissue cell cultures and in macaques. In the past, the vpu gene has not been considered as an important gene for pathogenesis because of lack of experimental evidence. Examination of the genetic mutations which occurred during the course of successive passages of non-pathogenic SHIV through monkey bone marrow, and the onset of pathogenicity reveals important information as to the genetic changes which lead to pathogenic SHIV such as SHIVKU_,. This examination has shown that while a functional vpu is most likely not the sole determinant of viral pathogenicity/virulence, it is however required that the vpu gene must become functional before other mutations could occur in either the e«v or nef genes and the subsequent development of pathogenic SHIV.

Recently it has been shown that the vpu gene product may play an important role in down-regulation of the expression of MHC class I molecules, and thereby contribute to the inability of CD8+ T cells to eradicate HIV-1 from infected individuals (Kerkau et al., J. Exp. Medicine 185(7): 1295-1305, 1997).

Certain aspects of the present invention will be better understood by the illustrated embodiments of the following examples. The following examples are meant by way of illustration and not by limitation. One of ordinary skill in the art will be able to understand and use the teaching of the present invention to make modifications and further embodiments which are still within the teaching, spirit and scope of the invention.
Example 1 Resistance to replication of SIVmac or avirulent SHIV, results in resistance to infection by SHIVKU_,

Twelve macaques who have developed immunological control over replication of SIV-... or avirulent SHIV, unexpectedly demonstrated resistance to SHIVKU_, infection. These animals had developed sterilizing immunity which prevented the establishment of infection
by SHIVKL . Thus these SIV-infected, and now resistant animals, resisted challenge by SHIVKLM virus which has human HIV-1 envelope. Since the envelope of SIVmac (which is closely related to the env of HIV-2) is distinct from the env of HIV-1, the resistance of these animals to infection by SHIVKU_, suggests that questions about effectiveness of vaccines being compromised by the inherent variability in wild-type HIV viruses is in operation a non- issue.

Example 2 SHIVKU_, infects across mucosal membranes
Sexually mature macaques inoculated intravaginally with SHIVKU_, rapidly developed systemic and CNS infection and disease manifested by intense proliferation of the virus, precipitous and permanent loss of CD4+ T cells, and development of AIDS. Analysis of the viral infection indicates that the rapid kinetics of the virus invasion across mucosal surfaces shows that local post-exposure prophylactic measures, such as anti-viral douches, must be implemented before two days post infection, since by 2 days post infection virus has reached the regional lymph nodes. In a similar vein, it is found that systemic dissemination of virus has occurred by day 4 post infection, and CNS infection has occurred by day 7, thus antiviral therapeutic intervention after day 4 may not prevent the establishment of systemic infection.

Example 3 Δ2 SHIV Vaccine

The Δ2 SHIV virus was constructed (with the nef and vpu genes deleted from SHIV- 4) and characterized in macaque cell cultures as to the genetic identity, confirmed by sequence analysis of genomic DNA. The nef anά vpu genes could be completely deleted or only partially deleted, or rendered non-functional by insertion of DNA into the gene, with the objective being that no functional nef or vpu gene product is produced. The Δ2 SHIV virus was inoculated subcutaneously into six adult female macaques. All six animals produced antibodies detectable by immunoprecipitation with SHIVKL virus by three months after initial inoculation. By five months after initial inoculation, all six animals were producing neutralizing antibodies to SHIVKU„, virus measuring with a response of 1 in 10 to 1 in 20.

At six months after initial inoculation, all six animals were healthy and showed no manifestations of AIDS pathology. Monthly analysis of blood cells via FACS (Fluorescence activated cell sorting) showed that the six animals were free from AIDS pathology. Virus was no longer detectable in blood mononuclear cells by six months after initial inoculation, as detectable by infectivity assays and by PCR analysis. Subsequently, at about six months after initial inoculation, the six inoculated animals and two un-vaccinated control animals were challenged by intravaginal administration of SHIVKU.| virus. The animals were evaluated for presence of infectious cells, and for their CD4+ cell count. Generally, as an assay for virus infectivity the frequency of infectious cells was measured by inoculation of serial 10-fold dilutions of PBMC (peripherial bone marrow cells, in particular blood mononuclear cells) or other cells onto indicator cells in 24-well tissue culture plates, which were then observed for development of syncytial CPE (cytopathic effects) during a 7-day period. Then lOOμl from each well was transferred to another plate, fresh indicator cells added (human T cell line C8166) , and the plates were then observed for
a further 7 days. Routinely 106 cells from each animal were used for estimation of infectivity, and reported as number of infectious cells per 106 cells.

Cell counts were generally determined using FACS (fluorescence-activated cell sorting) where cells were reacted with mAb to CD4 (SIM.4, NIH AIDS research and Reagents repository), or CD8 (Dako T8, Dako). After washing, the cells were stained with FITC-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (Dako), fixed in 1% buffered formalin, and analyzed on a fluorescence-activated cell counter. Example 4 Avpu PPc SHIV Vaccine

SHIV PPc is a non-pathogenic SHIV generated from animal PPc during the course of sequential passage through bone marrow as descibed previously (see Figure 5). Modification of the parental SIV virus, was done to incorporate HIV-1 vpu, nef and env to create a SHIV. It was found that this modified parental SHIV was actually not pathogenic. Inoculation of this modified parental SHIV into two macaques demonstrated that the virus was avirulent, and could result in the generation of immunity to the virus. However, this virus retained the full potential to become a pathogenic virus. Thus in order to prevent this type of mutation and create a safer vaccine, deletion of the vpu gene was made which resulted in Avpu PPc SHIV. The inactivation of the vpu gene can be accomplished by complete deletion of the vpu gene, partial deletion of portions of the vpu gene, or it could be rendered non- functional by insertion of DNA, the objective being to inactivate the gene such that no functional vpu gene product is present. In order to prevent mutation of the altered vpu gene back into a functional gene, complete deletion of the vpu gene may be preferred.

Example 5 HIV-1 Vaccine

Because of their SIVmac content (LTR, gag, pol, and nef), Avpu PPc SHIV and Δ2 SHIV do not replicate efficiently in human cells, and thus while useful as vaccines in humans, may not generate complete immunity. Using the teachings of the results from Avpu PPc SHIV and Δ2 SHIV, it is proposed that a human HIV-1 vaccine be constructed by using HIV-2 as the substitute for the SHIV component of the validated model vaccines.

In one embodiment, construction of an effective human vaccine would involve combining the LTR, gag, pol, and nef genes of HIV-2 in the same arrangement as in SIN^.,
with the genes of HIV-1 to construct a purely human HIV counterpart to the Avpu SHIVKU., and Δ2 SHIV virus vaccines. In one embodiment the genes of HIV-2 is combined in the same arrangement as in SIVmac, of course it is also possible to combine the genes in the natural order as found in HIV-2, or in different order or orientations. However, the genes should be expressed in a fashion as to allow for the generation of an effective immune response in the inoculated subject. Thus in one form of this embodiment a HIV-2 virus is used to provide the background of genes, and the HIV-1 env, tat, rev, vpu genes are substituted into this background of HIV-2 genes. As taught above, it may be preferred not to transfer the vpu gene, or at minimum to transfer and render non-functional the vpu gene. The human HIV vaccines can undergo preliminary testing in human cell cultures of lymphocytes and macrophages for evidence of infection and any retained pathogenicity. These virus constructs can also be tested in monkeys, such as chimpanzees and macaques, for evidence of replication.

In one embodiment, construction of an effective human vaccine would involve rendering non-functional the vpu gene in an HIV-1 virus. Optionally, the nef gene can also be rendered non-functional or deleted. Interestingly, it has been found that the vpu gene in many HIV-1 cultured virus is inactivated (Vaishnav & Wong-Staal, 1991, supra.), but as shown by the results here, activation of vpu in these HIV-1 culture stocks will create pathogenic virulent HIV-1. Thus it is preferred, to make a safe vaccine, that the vpu gene be rendered inactive by deletion of some or all of the gene from the virus DNA, preferably where the vpu gene has been deleted completely.

Example 6 In Vivo vaccination against sexually-transmitted HIV disease SHIVKL , bearing the envelope of HIV-1, causes fulminant infection with sub-total loss of CD4+ T cells and AIDS in intravaginally-inoculated macaques. This virus and route of inoculation was used to challenge six adult macaques immunized seven months previously by subcutaneous injection with attenuated AvpuAnef SHIV-4. The animals developed neutralizing antibodies to SHIV, but only minimally-detectable cell mediated immune responses. Two unvaccinated controls and one vaccinate succumbed to challenge, but five of six vaccinates developed only
transient infection with the virulent virus and have remained healthy, without CD4* T cell loss. This is the first demonstration of protection against virulent SHIV administered by the intravaginal route. These results support the concept that sexually-transmitted HIV disease can be prevented by immunization. HIV-1 is primarily a sexually transmitted virus that causes persistent systemic infection and loss of CD4+ T cells. The infection culminates in loss of immunocompetence and development of AIDS. Although several effective anti-HIV drugs, notably viral protease inhibitors, are now available, their widespread use is hampered by their high cost and the need for multiple treatments daily for an indefinite period. Their use is thus not feasible in less developed countries where the bulk of HIV infections occur. Under these conditions, development of a safe and effective vaccine is a priority. Moreover, such a vaccine should protect against the sexually transmitted virus. The inability of HIV-1 to infect animals other than chimpanzees has meant that macaque models using non-human primate lentiviruses have become the only practical alternative for testing proof-of-concept approaches to vaccines against HIV-1.

SIVmac, which is closely related to HIV-2 and SIVsm, causes AIDS in macaques and has been extensively used in vaccine studies. Macaques vaccinated with attenuated strains of SIVmac, produced by deleting auxiliary genes, particularly nef, resisted infection after challenge with virulent strains of SIVmac (Daniel, M. D., Kirchhoff, F., Czajak, S. C, Sehgal, P. K. & Desrosiers, R. C. Science 258, 1938-1941 (1992); Almond, N., Kent, K., Cranage, M., Rud, E., Clarke, B. & Stott, E. J. Lancet 345, 1342-1344 (1995); Stahl Hennig, C, Dittmer, U., Nisslein, T., et al. J. Gen. Virol. 77, 2969-2981 (1996); Wyand, M. S., Manson, K. H., Garcia Moll, M., Montefiori, D. & Desrosiers, R. C. J. Virol. 70, 3724-3733 (1996)). A major limitation of the SIV model of AIDS in macaques is that this virus is only distantly related to HIV-1 genetically, and although SIVmac does cause AIDS, the biological properties of SIVmac vary greatly from those of HIV-1. Therefore, vaccine-induced responses which protect against virulent SIVnιac in macaques may or may not be directly applicable to HIV-1. Since some of the differences in the biological properties of these viruses are
attributable to their envelope glycoproteins, chimeric simian-human immunodeficiency virus (SHIV) which contains the core of SIVmac and the envelope glycoprotein of HIV-1 was created to address this question. Newly created SHIVs were infectious but not pathogenic and thus vaccines could not be evaluated for efficacy in preventing disease. The recent derivation of virulent SHIV (SHIVKU.,) which causes almost total loss of CD4+ T cells and AIDS in macaques in six months after inoculation established a new and reproducible model which accurately reflected HIV-1 disease compressed in a short time frame (Joag, S. V., Li, Z., Foresman, L., et al. J. Virol. 70, 3189-97. (1996); Joag, S. V., Li, Z., Foresman, L., et al. AIDS Res. Hum. Retroviruses 13, 635-645 (1997); Joag, S. V., Adany, I., Li, Z., et al. J. Virol. 71, 4016-4023 (1997)). Moreover, the new virus is virulent after intravenous, oral, or intravaginal infusion. This virus thus proved ideal for evaluating efficacy of vaccines. The choice of a live-virus vaccine was based on observations of genetic changes occurring in the virus during animal passages which yielded SHIVKU_,. The original molecularly cloned SHIV-4 is avirulent and the vpu gene does not encode a functional protein. SHIVKU., which is extremely virulent, encodes a functional Vpu and has amino acid substitutions in other viral proteins, including gρl60, Nef, Tat, Rev and Vpr (Stephens, E. B., Joag, S. V., Sheffer, D., et al. J. Med. Primatol. 25, 175-185 (1996); Stephens, E. B., Mukherjee, S., Sahni, M., et al. Virology 231, 313-321 (1997)). Assuming that development of virulence of SHIVKL was multifactoral (i.e., associated with amino acid changes in multiple viral proteins) including changes in vpu and nef genes, both genes from original SHIV-4 were deleted to develop a vaccine.

Discussion

These results show that a vaccine which caused subclinical and minimally productive infection in macaques, induced protection in 5/6 animals against loss of CD4+ T cells and AIDS after intravaginal infusion of virulent SHIVKLM. This is the first demonstration that sexually transmitted HIV-1 disease caused by a lentivirus bearing the envelope of HIV-1 could be averted by immunization. The success of the vaccine experiment was defined by the virulence of the challenge virus. This is an extremely virulent virus which shares the envelope of HIV-1 and causes HIV-1 disease, including loss of CD4+ T cells and AIDS, in a predictable manner during a six-month course of infection, even after intravaginal infusion of virus. The fact that the vaccinates were protected against this virus shows that not only could HIV-1 disease be prevented by immunization, but that the protection extended to sexually transmitted disease.

The two sham-inoculated control animals challenged with SHIVKU_, succumbed predictably to the challenge virus, having developed massive systemic infection and subtotal loss of CD4+ T cells with viremia and viral antigenemia soon after challenge. This sequence of events had been observed in numerous other animals as reported earlier. The fact that all six of the vaccinates developed systemic infection with the challenge virus showed that the virus had breached the vaginal mucosal barrier and had reached the draining lymph nodes, as confirmed by PCR on PBMC and mesenteric lymph nodes. In an earlier study on pathogenesis of SHIV-infection after intravaginal infusion of the virus, it was shown that soon after virus became detectable in mesenteric lymph nodes, an explosive burst of virus replication ensued in the lymphoid tissues. However, in the vaccinates reported here, virus replication was completely suppressed in three (PDj, PLk and PNa) since no infectious virus could be recovered from lymph node or PBMC cells despite presence of challenge virus DNA. The other two vaccinates, 42105 and PPm that resisted the virus had very low number of infectious cells, 5 and 10 cells/106 PBMC, even though these animals had large number of susceptible CD4+ T cells. This indicated failure of the virus to replicate and spread among
susceptible cells. Vaccinate 42107 which succumbed to AIDS had an unanticipated high virus burden, similar to the control animals. It is of interest that both of the vaccinates, 42105 and 42107, that became productively infected with SHIV^., developed partial loss of CD4+ T cells shortly after challenge. Infections in these two animals had diametrically opposite outcomes, since macaque 42105 gradually gained control over the virus with restoration of CD4+ T cell values, whereas in 42107 there was a slowly progressive loss of the CD4+ T cells that ended in development of AIDS. Thus, only one of the six animals developed disease following exposure to the challenge virus.

Our results are in keeping with the precedent that SIVmac-induced AIDS in macaques could be prevented by prior infection with SIV whose virulence had been attenuated by deletion of accessory genes including nef. This converted virulent SIV to an avirulent virus, which was then used as a vaccine. In this case, the rationale for the vaccine constructs differed from that of SIV. SIV does not have a vpu gene. During the development of virulence in SHIV by animal to animal passage the vpu gene became functional prior to acquisition of most of the mutations in the env and nef genes which are present in virulent SHIVKU.,. This led to the speculation that deletion of the two accessory genes, vpu and nef, would prevent development of virulence. The strategy worked. Whether deletion of the vpu gene alone in this vaccine construction would have sufficed is not known.

While the precise mechanisms associated with development of vaccine-induced resistance to replication of SHIVKU_, are not fully understood, it is clear that the vaccine virus had replicated sufficiently in the animals to induce binding antibodies to both the SIV gag and the HIV-1 envelope proteins and neutralizing antibodies to SHIVKU_,. New results showed that passively-immunized macaques having antibodies with similar titers in their plasma as the vaccinates were refractory to infection with virulent SHIV. Thus, presence of neutralizing antibodies alone may have been capable of averting productive infection with SHIVKU_, in the vaccinates. Interestingly, macaque 42107 had developed neutralizing antibodies to SHIVKU., at 10 and 6 weeks prior to challenge but the neutralizing titer had dropped to an undetectable level at the time of challenge. This macaque went on to develop
productive infection with SHIV and development of AIDS even though the neutralizing antibody titer rose again. Presence of these antibodies prior to challenge may be protective but not after infection.

The apparent lack of SHIV-specific proliferative responses in and CTL activity PBMC from the vaccinates was surprising. These results are in striking contrast to the high T cell proliferative activity previously documented in HIV- 1 -infected chimpanzees (Nehete, P. N., Murthy, K. K., Satterfield, W. C, Arlinghaus, R. B. & Sastry, K. J. _ 7E>S 9, 567-572 (1995)) and in rhesus macaques immunized with HIV-1 gpl60-derived peptides (Nehete, P. N., Satterfield, W. C, Matherne, C. M., Arlinghaus, R. B. & Sastry, K. J. AIDS Res. Hum. Retroviruses 9, 235-240 (1993)). However, the results are in concordance with the similar low levels of CTL activity directed against SIV-RT and SW-nef reported to contribute to protection of macaques against mucosal challenge with SIV (Putkonen, P., Makitalo, B., Bottiger, D., Biberfeld, G. & Thorstensson, R. J. Virol. 71, 4981-4984 (1997)). Additionally, since proliferative and CTL responses in lymph node cells were not analized, it cannot exclude the presence of SHIV-specific cellular immune mechanisms in the vaccinated monkeys since the immune cells may have been confined to the lymphoid tissues. That CMI responses may have been involved in resistance to SHIV-disease comes from earlier studies in which macaques that had recovered from infection with macrophage-tropic SIV were refractory to superinfection with SHIV (Stephens, E. B., Joag, S. V., Atkinson, B., et al. Virology 234, 328-339 (1997)). The envelope glycoprofiens of these two viruses are distinctly different and, as expected, serum from the SIV-infected animals failed to neutralize SHIV, yet the animals resisted infection by SHIV. Future studies on CMI responses to vaccine virus using lymph node cells will shed new light on this problem. However, although the mechanisms of protection against SHIVKU_, are not understood fully, the results clearly shows that sexually transmitted HIV-1 disease can be averted by vaccination.

Example 9 Oral Immunization

Six adult macaques were immunized subcutaneously with vaccine 1 (ΔvpuΔnef), and six were immunized orally with vaccine 2 (Δvpu). Both viruses caused infection in all inoculated animals, but whereas vaccine 1 virus caused only a nonproductive type of infection, vaccine 2 virus replicated productively but transiently for a 6- to 10-week period.

Both groups were challenged 6-7 months later with pathogenic SHIVKU_, by the intravaginal route. All four unvaccinated controls developed low CD4+ T-cell counts (<200/μl) and AIDS. The 12 vaccinated animals all became infected with SHIVKU_,, and two in group 1 developed a persistent productive infection followed by development of AIDS in one. The other 10 have maintained almost complete control over virus replication even though spliced viral RNA was detected in lymph nodes. This suppression of virus replication correlated with robust antiviral cell-mediated immune responses. This is the first demonstration of protection against virulent SHIV administered by the intravaginal route. This study supports the concept that sexually transmitted HIV diseases can be prevented by parental or oral immunization.

Neutralizing antibody assays were conducted as in Example 6.

Detection of viral DNA in tissues. Tissues from inoculated animals were first screened for the presence of the SIV region of SHIV by PCR using oligonucleotide primers specific for both SIV and SHIV. The gαg-specific oligonucleotides and the conditions for amplification were exactly as described previously (Joag et al. 1994. Virology 300:436-446). The result of this PCR was the

Lymphocyte proliferation assay. PBMC from different macaques, collected 49 weeks after virus challenge, were cultured in triplicate as 106 cells/well in 96-well tissue culture dishes in 200 μl of RPMI 1640 containing 10% FBS. Stock SHIVKU., (104 2TCID /ml) was UV irradiated for 30 minutes and heat treated at 56°C for 60 min before use as antigen; 20μl of this material was added to each well. Three wells each containing unstimulated PBMC from different pig-tailed macaques served as negative controls. Cells were cultured for 6 days before the addition to each well of 1 μCi of [3H]thymidine (Specific activity, 247.9 GBq/minol, NEN, Boston, MA). Cultures were harvested onto glass fiber filter mats by using an automated plate harvester (Skatron, Sterling, VA) 24 h after addition of [3H]thymidine, and [3H]thymidine incorporation was determined with a Microbeta liquid scintillation counter (Packard). Stimulation index (SI) was calculated as mean counts per
minute in stimulated wells/mean counts per minute in control well, and an SI of greater than 1.5 was considered significant (Buge et al. 1997. J. Virol. 71:8531-8541.).

Development of CD4+ T cell clones. CD4" cells from group 1 macaques PDj and Pna (week 50 post-challenge) were negatively selected from PBMC first by incubating PBMC with mouse anti-human CD8 monoclonal antibody and then with anti-mouse Immunoglobulin G magnetic beads (Dynal, Lake Success, N.Y.). Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 89:31 16-31 19). CD4+ T cell clones were derived from the limiting-dilution method and the phenotype was confirmed by staining with mouse anti-human CD4" antibody. PDj and PNa PBMC were collected 50 weeks after virus challenge and co- cultured with UV-irradiated SHIVKL -infected autologues CD4+ T cells (effector/stimulator ratio of 10:1) in 24-well tissue culture plates in RPMI 1640 containing 10% FBS. They were restimulated on day 7 and used as effectors on day 14 in a chromium release assay.

Target cells (autologues CD4 T cell close) were either infected with SHIVKU., or sham infected for 3 days and then used in chromium release assays. Cells were labeled with 100 μCi 51Cr (specific activity, 962 MBq/ml of sodium chromate (Amershan, Cleveland, OH) for 2 h and then washed thrice with Hanks balanced salt solution. Target cells (2,500/well) were dispensed in triplicate and effector cells added in triplicate in effector/target (E/T) ratios of 80, 40, 20, 10, and 5 into each well of 96-well U-bottom plates. Chromium release was determined after 4 hours of incubation at 37°C in a 5% CO2 incubator. Plates were spun at 1 ,200 rpm for 5 minutes, and 100 μl of supernatant from each well was counted in a gamma counter (Packard, Meridian, Con.). Each experiment had three wells containing only targets and medium that provided the data for spontaneous release, while three wells containing targets and 5% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) served as wells for maximal release of
chromium. The percent specific cytotoxity was calculated as (test release — spontaneous release) divided by (maximum release — spontaneous release) x 100. Spontaneous lysis of relevant control target was always less than 25% of maximum release.

The two unvaccinated controls developed the typical massive infection caused by SHIVKU.,. Biopsy and examination of axillary lymph nodes from five of the six vaccinated macaques at 18 weeks showed an open vpu gene in three (Table 15), demonstrating that the animals had become infected with SHIVKU_,. However, as for the four macaques in group 1, virus was recovered only rarely from PBMC of these vaccinated macaques at any time point. The animals have remained healthy and failed to develop virus- associated loss of CD4+ T cells during more than 40 weeks of examination. Considerable menstrual blood loss among these retired breeders, especially 8124, appeared to be associated with the wide fluctuations of CD4+ T-cell counts in individuals. Whatever the reason for loss of these cells, it was not associated with virus replication (Tables 12 and 15). Thus, although all six had become infected with virus crossing the vaginal mucosa and entering the regional lymph nodes, no systemic productive viral replication ensued in any of them. At 27 and 35 weeks post-challenge, plasma RNA levels in the six vaccinated macaques were less that 600 and 300 copies/ml, respectively, whereas the surviving unvaccinated challenge control animal had 490,000 copies/ml (Table 14).

Since nearly all of the animals receiving either vaccine had undetectable levels of virus in the plasma, we sought to determine the status of virus replication in lymph nodes. Studies of HIV-infected people have shown that replication-competent virus can be rescued from lymph nodes (Chun et al. 1997. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 94: 13193-13197; Finzi et al. 1997. Science 278: 1295-1300; Wong et al. 1997. Science 278: 1291-1295), and active virus replication can be demonstrated in lymph nodes with the use of primers for spliced mRNAs, even while the plasma has less than 400 copies of viral RNA/ml (Gunthard et al. 1998. J. Virol. 72:2422-2428). Since lymph nodes of vaccinated macaques contained pro viral DNA of the challenge virus, SHIVKU_,, we considered it important to determine whether the virus was inactive (trapped in follieular dendritic cells) or was replicating. Lymph node RNA was prepared from biopsies obtained from all surviving 11 of the 12 vaccinated macaques at weeks 54 and 60 (group 1) and weeks 31 and 37 (group 2). RT-PCR amplification of lymph node RNA from the five vaccinated macaques of group 1, using
primers to the SIV pol gene, did not reveal detectable SHIV after 35 cycles despite obvious low-grade infection in PBMC of 42105 (Table 14). However, the RNA from the lymph node of 42105 was not of good quality, as shown by the lack of GAPDH signal. The one remaining unvaccinated challenged animal, Pfy, showed a strong signal in the initial reaction with the outer primers. However, lymph nodes of four of the five vaccinated macaques in group 1 did show a specific signal upon nested set amplification of 34 further cycles. In group 2, again, only the unvaccinated animal showed a signal upon the initial RT-PCR (not shown), but five of the six vaccinated animals (the exception being 42106) showed a signal upon nested set amplification. These assays detected full-length mRNAs. Since these could have been viral RNA in virion particles trapped in the lymph nodes, we used a different set of primers spanning the introns of the tat and rev genes to detect multiply spliced viral mRNAs, indicative of replication. The two remaining unvaccinated challenge animals (Pfy and PDb) and 1 of the 1 1 vaccinated macaques (macaque 42105 in group 1) had a detectable signal with these primers. However, nested PCR showed that two other group 1 animals (PD and PPm) and 3 group animals (8124, 42106, and PWv;) had positive signals (summarized in Table 14). Thus, virus replication, albeit at an extremely low level, was still in progress in three of the five vaccinated macaques in group 1 and three of the six in group 2.

Since virus replication was in progress in the lymphoid tissues but had been kept in check in 10 of the 12 vaccinated macaques, we sought to determine whether the vaccinated macaques had developed anti-viral cell-mediated immune (CMI) responses. We determined first whether the animals had acquired virus-specific T-helper (Th) cells by using assays for lymphocyte proliferation after exposure of PBMC to virus.

Four of the five macaques in group 1 and all six macaques in group 2 displayed moderate to excellent responses when stimulated in vitro with inactivated challenge virus (Table 16), suggesting that major hisotcompatibility complex class Il-restricted antiviral Th cells may have been expanded in these vaccinated macaques. The single surviving unvaccinated challenge control animal, PDb, failed to display any significant proliferation of T cells in vitro. It is thus of interest that this animal, which had DNA of both vaccine and challenge viruses in it lymph node and had controlled virus replication completely, showed no significant proliferation of T cells. In contrast, macaque 42105, the only member of the group that had an ongoing productive infection, had the highest SI value. Primed relevant Th cells were detected in all of the vaccinated macaques in group 2. While SI values may not be markers of resistance to virus replication, they may contribute to the development of such resistance.

DISCUSSION

Six sexually mature macaques inoculated orally on a single occasion with ΔvpuSHIVpp. (group 2) developed an uneventful, transiently productive infection that conferred protection against AIDS caused by intravaginally inoculated, highly virulent SHIVKU_, (χ2 test, P = 0.005. All four of the unvaccinated control macaques inoculated intravaginally with this virus developed highly productive infection, subtotal loss of CD4+ T cells, and AIDS, confirming our finding (Joag et al. 1997. J. Virol. 71 :4016-4023) on development of disease in six of six animals that became infected after nontraumatic intravaginal infection of this virus. The first vaccine virus, pvpupnefSHI V-4, was incapable
of causing infection after mucosal inoculation (and therefore was injected subcutaneously) and replicated poorly in all six macaques, but nevertheless induced binding and neutralizing antibodies to the virus, proving infection. Four of these six vaccinated macaques resisted productive infection and disease following intravaginal challenge with SHIVKLM (χ2 test, P = 0.102). Of the two animals that developed productive infection, one developed AIDS and another remains at risk of developing AIDS. Given this prognosis, ony 2 of the 12 vaccinated macaques, compared to four of four of the control animals, developed disease (2 test, P = 0.003). These results demonstrated that sexually transmitted disease caused by HIV-1 in human beings can probably be prevented by prophylactic immunization. Both vaccine viruses caused persistent infection irrespective of whether they replicated productively during the first few weeks following inoculation. Six months following immunization, even though infectious virus could no longer be isolated from PBMC from any of the 12 vaccinated macaques, vaccine virus DNA was still detectable. All 12 animals had developed binding and very low neutralizing antibody titers to SHIVKU_, in plasma by the time of virus challenge (approximately 6 months following vaccination). As shown, all 12 became infected with the challenge virus, since its DNA was clearly detectable in PBMC or mesenteric lymph node a few months following challenge. Two of the six vaccinated macaques in group 1 developed a persistent productive infection in PBMC and one, 42107, succumbed to AIDS approximately 6 months following challenge. The other macaque, 42105, had a phase of low-grade productive infection for 30 weeks followed by a 12-week period when it had no circulating infections PBMC in blood. However, from week 50 onward, infectious PBMC, accompanied by relatively low concentrations of viral RNA (5,000 to 70,000, versus 4 X 105 to 3 X 106 in controls) have reappeared in blood. At 60 weeks post-challenge, this animal still has large numbers of uninfected CD4+ T cells (which are highly susceptible to infection), in contrast to control animals, nearly all of whose CD4+ T cells became infected and eliminated during the first 3 weeks of infection. Nevertheless, the resurgence of virus in macaque 42105 suggests that this animal may be at risk for developing late-onset AIDS.
The other 10 vaccinated macaques, 4 in group 1 and all six in orally immunized group 2, developed a unique type of control over replication of SHIVKU.,. Rarely and transiently, small numbers of infectious cells have appeared in blood, but at nearly all time points, replication-competent virus could not be isolated from PBMC or lymph (sampled two to three times during this period of observations) by any procedure. Attempts have included three successive cocultivations of CD8-depleted PBMC with mitogen-activated normal PBMC or T cell lines. Nevertheless, both viral DNA and viral RNA have persited in lymph node tissue. Further, the detection of spliced viral RNA in lymph nodes of few animals in both groups suggested that an extremely low level of replication of SHIVKU_, has probably been in progress continuously in all of the vaccinated macaques. This type of replication of SHIVKU_, has probably been in progress continuously in all of the vaccinated macaques. This type of replication of this virus had never been observed before. We have previously demonstrat4ed (see above) that viral DNA became detectable by day 2 after inoculation of mesenteric lymph nodes and that explosive replication of the agent occurred during the following week. In this study, although the intravaginal route of inoculation was shown to be about 30-fold less sensitive than the intravenous route, all animals that became infected after intravaginal inoculation nevertheless developed disease. Extrapolating these data to our vaccinated macaques, since all had developed infection in lymph nodes, we surmised that systemic rather than mucosal factors were responsible for curtailment of virus replication. It is doubtful that neutralizing antibodies had a significant role in curtailment of virus replication in the vaccinated macaques. In an earlier report (Foresman et al. AIDS Res. Hum. Retroviruses 14:1035-1043), we showed that passively administered immune serum was effective only when given before parental inoculation of the virus. This serum had no therapeutic effect when given 2 h following virus inoculation. Worse still, unlike the success at preventing infection after parental inoculation of the virus, we were unable to protect macaques from the dire effects of infection by infusing the serum 24 h before mucosal inoculation of the agent. Immune serum therefore had no apparent effect on an already established infection, a well-known phenomenon in lentivirus infections, nor apparently
could the previously administered serum prevent infection across mucosal surfaces. Restriction of virus replication in our 10 vaccinated macaques must therefore have been mediated by factors other than neutralizing antibodies.

Studies on CMI responses of the vaccinated macaques have only recently begun. That this type of immunity is important came from an earlier finding that macaques that had "recovered" from infection with virulent SIVmac were protected from effects of infection with SHIVKU_, (Stephens et al. 1997. Virology 234:328-339). Since these two viruses have distinctly different envelopes, the protection was probably mediated by CMI responses to viral core proteins shared by the two viruses. In the present study, our findings that CD4+ T cells in the vaccinated macaques at week 50 in group 1 and in week 30 in group 2 proliferated when exposed to antigens of SHIVKlw, showed that the animals had developed anti-SHIV CMI responses that have persisted along with the infection. The further preliminary finding that 2 of the 10 vaccinated macaques that have controlled virus replication have developed CTL to the virus has strengthened the premise that CMI responses are responsible for control and curtailment of replication of the virulent virus. Possibly, a dynamic interaction between virus replication and CTL curtailment responses is continuously at play. A recent study of CTL responses in HIV-infected humans showed an inverse correlation between the levels of CTL and plasma viral RNA loads (Musey et al. 1997. N. Engl. J. Med. 337:1267-1274), implicating a role for CTL control of viral replication and delay of disease progression.
Example 10. Reduction in challenge virus DNA burden

HIV-1 causes both highly productive and clinically latent phases of infection, but vaccination approaches have focused primarily on prevention of the former. We used the SHIVKU_, macaque model of HIV infection/disease to investigate the feasibility of vaccine prevention of both parameters of infection. Using an oral vaccine, Δ-vpuSHIVPPc (V-virus), we show that vaccinated animals became infected in lymph nodes with challenge virus SHIVKL (C-virus), but productive C-virus replication was suppressed. DNA of both V- and C-viruses persisted in lymph nodes of all six animals, but during the second year after
challenge, four of the six animals lost the C-virus DNA signal. This was associated with persistence of V-virus and prominent CTL responses. This is the first demonstration that vaccination against a pathogenic primate lentivirus can cause reduction of challenge virus burden, including its DNA intermediate phase in lymph nodes. This suggests that a reduction in the level of challenge virus DNA could be included among the efficacy requirements of an HIV vaccine.

The ultimate goal of all viral vaccines is to emulate the specific immunity that heralds the end of infection by pathogenic viruses (Murphy BR & Chanock RM. Immunization against virus disease. In Fields Virology (Ed. Fields, B.N.et al.) 467-97 (Lippincott-Raven, New York, 1996). Application of this concept to HIV-1 creates a theoretical stumbling block for vaccine development because, in most cases of HIV infection, specific immunity to the virus causes reduction in viral replication, but it does not eliminate viral DNA from cellular reservoirs in lymph nodes where it is thought to cause latent infection. (Chun, T.W. et al. Nature 387, 183-8 (1997)) A large number of vaccines have been tested in the SIV-macaque model of HIV infection and pathogenesis, and claims of success have been based on prevention or delay in disease onset, or reduction of productive virus replication, but none has yet approached the question of elimination of DNA of the challenge virus from lymph nodes.

To explore the question of limits of protection against replication of challenge virus, we inoculated two groups of six pig-tailed macaques with two live vaccines, ΔvpuΔnefSHIV- 4 (vaccine 1 , or V-I) and ΔvpuSHIVPPc (vaccine 2, or V-II), respectively, and challenged them by vaginal inoculation with SHIVKU_, (C-virus) six months later. MATERIALS AND METHODS

Identification of vaccine virus and challenge virus DNA sequences by PCR amplification of the vpu region. DNA was isolated from lymph node tissue or PBMC by standard procedures The vpu/gpl20 regions of viral genomes were amplified by nested PCR that produces fragments diagnostic for either vaccine virus DNA or challenge virus DNA as described above. After the second round of amplification, challenge virus DNA, which has an intact vpu gene, yields a fragment of 431 bp while vaccine virus DNA, with a 60 base pair
deletion in the vpu gene, yields a fragment of 371 bp. Amplification of each sample was repeated 4 times in separate reactions to ensure accuracy.

Virus recovery from lymph nodes. Lymph node cells were obtained from mesenteric lymph node tissue and CD4* cells were negatively selected using immunomagnetic beads as described above. The CD4* cells were counted, stimulated with PHA (lμg/ml) for 48 hr, and 2 xlO6 cells were co-cultured with 1 x 106 C8166 indicator cells. After co-cultivation for 7 days, the cultures were examined for CPE.

Lymphocyte proliferation assay. PBMC from different macaques, collected at week 98 or 99 post-challenge, were cultured in triplicate in the presence or absence of UV irradiated and heat inactivated SHIVKU_, for 4 days. Cells were then pulsed with lμCi [3H] thymidine for 18 hours before being subjected to scintillation spectroscopy. Stimulation indices were calculated as mean counts per minute (CPM) in stimulated wells/mean CPM in control wells.

Generation of bulk CTL population and chromium release assay. CTL activity was determined as described elsewhere12. Briefly, CTL effectors were prepared by stimulating PBMCs from different macaques with UV irradiated autologous CD4+ T cells infected with SHIVKL . Autologous CD4+ T cells infected with SHIVKU_, or autologous B cells infected with recombinant vaccinia virus expressing HIVenv or SIVgag or SIVpol were used as targets in 4 hr. chromium release assay. The percent specific cytotoxicity was calculated as (test release- spontaneous release)/(maximum release-spontaneous release) X 100.

Initially, four unvaccinated control macaques developed typical acute infection with subtotal loss of CD4+ T cells within one month, and also subsequently developed AIDS. All twelve vaccinates became infected in lymph nodes with C-virus and infection spread to peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) in some of the animals during the early weeks following challenge. Two animals in the V-I group developed a slowly progressive infection that culminated in AIDS. The other four in the group eventually curtailed replication of the
virus in PBMC and remained healthy with normal levels of CD4* T cells. However, infectious C-virus was rescued from lymph node cells from three of these animals two years later. This indicated that the infection had regressed to a persistent, clinically latent stage in the lymph nodes. Among the animals in the V-II group, all six resisted productive replication of the virus and all have also remained healthy for more than two years. Furthermore, infectious SHIVKU., (C-virus) was rescueable from lymph node cells from only one of the six. Using primers that distinguish between the truncated vpu of the V-viruses and the full length vpu of C-virus, we monitored the animals for evidence of persistence of DNA of either or both viruses in PBMC and in lymph nodes, and compared these results with results regarding recovery of infectious virus from lymph node tissue from these animals. These data are summarized in Table 17. Animals were also monitored for humoral and cellular immune responses to C-virus. C-virus-antigen-specific CD4+T cells were detected in all ten animals throughout the post-challenge period between weeks 40 and 110. All ten surviving animals also had CTLs that recognized HIV env, and SIV gag and pol epitopes expressed by H. papio transformed B cells infected with recombinant vaccinia viruses. They also developed long- lasting CTLs directed against C-virus.

All four surviving animals in the V-I group had DNA of V- and C-viruses, and as mentioned above, C-virus was isolated from CD8"-depleted lymph node cells from three of the four at week 87. Examination of the V-II animals showed surprising results; V-virus was detected in all six animals throughout the post-challenge period up to the last timepoint at 103 weeks. Whereas all six animals in the VII group had C-virus DNA at week 18 post-challenge, the DNA signal for this virus became undetectable in one (PWv) at week 55, and in three others (PEy, PW1, and 7024) by week 63. The lack of C-virus DNA signal in lymph node and PBMC of the four animals was confirmed in tissue samples obtained at weeks 91 and 103. Thus, at the last time point sampled, 103 weeks post-challenge, four of the six animals showed only V-virus DNA. V-II-like viruses were isolated from CD8* depleted lymph node cells from two of these animals. Of the remaining two that had DNA of both viruses (42106 and 8124), lymph node cells from one (8124) yielded C-virus. Isolated viruses were identified by the presence or absence of vpu, and by nucleotide sequence analysis of gp\2Q and nef. Comparison of these sequences with those of V-II virus DNA and C-virus DNA showed that the newly isolated viruses have scattered mutations in gp\2Q and nef. The viruses isolated from PEy and PW1 in the V-II group are variants of V-II virus, and the agent isolated from 8124 is a variant of C-virus (data not shown). There was no evidence of recombination between V- and C-virus DNAs in any of the three newly derived agents.

The validity of the claim for reduction in C-virus DNA burden in the V-II animals is supported by the fact that a single set of primers was used to amplify both species of DNA. Because the primers bind to identical sites in both V-virus DNA and C-virus DNA, and the sequences of the amplified fragments differ only by a deletion of 60 bp, preferential amplification of one species was extremely unlikely. Effectively, the amplification of one species served as an internal control for the amplification of the other species. Thus, the detection of V-virus DNA and C-virus DNA in PBMC at week 55, and detection of only V- virus DNA in the four animals at 3 later time points, reflected an actual decline in the level of C-virus DNA in these animals. This finding is further supported by the failure to recover C- virus from any of these four animals.
The results from this study show that ten of the vaccinates not only resisted C-virus- mediated disease, but appeared to have gained control over productive replication by the virus, since CD4+ T cell counts in the animals were within normal ranges, their PBMC were devoid of infectious virus and viral DNA, and all ten had equivalent levels of cell-mediated immune responses to the virus.

Antiviral immunological responses of animals in the two groups provided no indication of the differences in effectiveness between the two vaccines. CD4+ T cells were equally responsive to viral antigens and CTLs recognized epitopes in all three of the structural proteins of the virus and in autologous CD4+ T cells infected with C-virus (Table 18). Although the study on CMI responses was not initiated until approximately 40 weeks post-challenge, this immune response was already in place in animals in both groups when, in the V-II group, not only had infectious virus been eliminated, but viral DNA was in the process of being eliminated in most of the animals. This contrasted with the V-I group in which infectious C-virus persisted. Thus, effector CTLs to the structural proteins of the virus did not determine whether or not infectious virus persisted in lymph nodes. It is possible that the sudden decline in the C viral DNA signal was associated with activation of replication of the vaccine virus since antigenically distinct vaccine viruses were obtained from 2 of the 4 vaccinates at 63 weeks. The success of the vaccine may have been due to its ability to replicate and concomitantly induce CTLs to both structural and non-structural proteins of the virus. This constellation of immune responses may be required for complete elimination of pathogenic virus.
